NOTE ON DECISION OF SUPREME COURT OF PAKISTAN (SCP) DATED JANUARY 26, 2024

INTRODUCTION

1.	This Note summarizes the implications arising out of SCP’s order dated January 26, 2024. 

2.	Through the above order, SCP has upheld the decision No.06 of 2019 dated September 6, 2021 pronounced by Hon’ble Sindh High Court (SHC) in case of M/s M. Mubashir Traders and others. 

BACKGROUND

3.	SHC, through its judgement dated September 6, 2021 dismissed the appeal filed by a distributor namely M/s M. Mubashir Traders (MT) of Colgate Palmolive (CP) against SRB Tribunal’s order dated November 22, 2018. SHC held that MT was not engaged in purchase and sale of goods; rather providing distribution service. Hence, MT’s revenue was subject to Sindh Sales Tax (SST) rather than Federal Sales Tax (FST).  SHC (and previously SRB Tribunal) have drawn their conclusions (that manufacturer exercise control over goods post delivery to distributor) on the basis of agreement between MT and CP, which (in their view) provides that: 

(i)	Manufacturer appointed the distributor for specific territory / area;

(ii) 	Distributor was assigned the responsibility of promotion of products and enhancement of sale;

(iii) 	Distributor was bound to maintain the adequate stock level;

(iv) 	Distributor was obligated to submit the periodic reports of stock to manufacturer;

(v) 	Manufacturer had discretion to buy back the unsold stock lying with distributor;

(vi) 	Distributor was bound to act upon the instruction of manufacturer regarding sale, price fixation and area / territory of sale;

(vii)  	Distributor was facilitating the manufacturer in making the sale; and 

(viii) 	The agreement between manufacturer and distributor enumerate the substance of service. 

3.1	The relevant extracts of the decision of SHC are enclosed as Annexure I to this note.





DECISION OF SCP AND ITS IMPLICATIONS 

4.	While SCP has not deliberated upon the matter in detail, it has simply upheld the findings of SHC which were based on the above elements / covenants of the contract between CP and MT. As a result, the transaction between manufacturer and distributor (in that case) has been adjudged as service arrangement and accordingly implications of SST would arise thereon under the category of ‘supply chain management or distribution (including delivery) services’ [tariff heading 9845.0000]. This would therefore result in non-applicability of FST for the reason that transaction would not be treated as ‘sale of goods’. 

The question arises whether after the pronouncement of decision of SCP, all the distribution arrangements would be treated as service arrangement? 

OUR OPINION

5.	In our view, the above decision cannot be applied (in general) on all the distribution arrangements. The implications of the above decision would apply on case to case basis, and be confined to those distribution contracts / arrangements where risk and rewards (i.e. title to the goods) are conditionally transferred with continuing control of manufacturer regarding decisions of pricing, discounts etc. In cases, where risk and rewards are transferred while manufacturer does not exercise control over the goods being transferred, the transaction can still be argued as subject to FST (and not SST).

6.	The disputes relating to determination of transaction of ‘sale of goods’ viz-a-viz services / agency arrangement have been subject to litigation in past. In this respect, we refer to the recent decision of SCP (2023 SCMR 1595) dated March 13, 2023 in case of M/s.Pak Saudi Fertilizers Limited. In that case, manufacturer engaged a marketing company to sell the goods to onward supply chain. Various tasks were required to be performed by the marketing company such as maintaining the quality of products, protect manufacturer against any harmful act, inspection of goods by manufacturer etc. Manufacturer was of the view that it had sold the goods to marketing company. The tax department treated it as agency relationship between manufacturer and marketing company. SCP in its decision deliberated upon the clauses of the agreement and held that transaction is an outright sale as it meets the criteria of sale of goods provided under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. The relevant extracts of the decision are enclosed as Annexure II. On similar dispute (relating to sale of goods versus agency) was settled by SHC vide its decision (No.ITC No.300/2004) dated October 22, 2020 in case of M/s.Brook Bond Pakistan Limited. In that case it was held that nomenclature of the agreement would not be relevant to determine the nature of transaction but the rule of substance over form would prevail. In that case too, the transaction was treated as sale of goods based on the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. We also enclose herewith the relevant extracts of said decision as Annexure III. 

7.	In addition to the above, we also refer to the decision of SCP (in CP No.243/2011 & CP No.1136/2018) dated May 31, 2022 in case M/s. Pakistan Tobacco Company Limited & Khurshid Ali (Pepsi Cola Dealer) wherein principles of sale of goods have been deliberated. SCP has drawn the inference from the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 and held that same meaning of ‘sale’ should be assigned to a transaction under the Sales Tax Act, 1990. It means that where risk and rewards are outrightly transferred from seller to the buyer, it would be construed as sale under the Sales Tax Act, 1990 as well. The relevant findings of the said decision are enclosed as Annexure IV to this note.

8.	We therefore consider that the recent decision of SCP (dated January 26, 2024) should be considered and applied in the context of terms of distributor agreement between CP and MT and other like similar agreement. The decision of SCP in our view is not in rem applicable to all distribution arrangement but based on the facts of the specific agreement. 

9.	It is therefore suggested that distribution agreements should be critically reviewed to assess whether the risk and rewards embedding in the goods are properly being transferred to distributors or not. If agreements enumerate that transactions fulfill the criteria of sale of goods as envisaged under the Sales of Goods Act, 1930 then FST would be applicable. However, if terms of the agreements reflect that sale of goods have not been executed (due to control of manufacturer) then implications of provincial taxes may arise.

   - Retailers: Retailers may have informal or formal agreements with suppliers, but they typically have more flexibility in sourcing products and may work with multiple suppliers simultaneously.

   - Retailers: Retailers may carry products from multiple brands and have more autonomy in how they present and market those products to consumers.

4. **Operational Support:**
   - Dealerships: Manufacturers often provide dealers with extensive support, including marketing materials, training programs, and operational assistance to maintain brand standards.
   - Retailers: Retailers operate more independently and may have fewer formal support mechanisms from suppliers. They are responsible for their own marketing, training, and operational activities.

5. **Inventory Management:**
   - Dealerships: Inventory management in dealerships is often tightly controlled, with manufacturers or distributors supplying products directly to dealers based on demand forecasts and sales agreements.
   - Retailers: Retailers manage their own inventory, sourcing products from various suppliers based on consumer demand, trends, and availability.

6. **Customer Relationship:**
   - Dealerships: Dealers often develop long-term relationships with customers, providing specialized knowledge, after-sales service, and support for the products they sell.
   - Retailers: Retailers serve a broad customer base and may focus on providing a wide range of products and services to meet diverse consumer needs.

   - Dealerships: The dealership model often involves a focus on specific product lines or industries, with dealers specializing in the sale and service of particular types of products.
   - Retailers: Retailers have a broader business model, offering a wide variety of products and services to appeal to different consumer segments and market niches.

MEMORANDUM REGARDING SUPREME COURT OF PAKISTAN (SCP) DECISION DATED JANUARY 26, 2024

INTRODUCTION

1. This memorandum provides an overview of the implications stemming from SCP's order dated January 26, 2024.

2. SCP's recent order upholds Decision No. 06 of 2019, rendered by the Hon’ble Sindh High Court (SHC) on September 6, 2021, concerning the case of M/s M. Mubashir Traders and others.

BACKGROUND

3. SHC, through its judgment dated September 6, 2021, dismissed the appeal filed by the distributor, M/s M. Mubashir Traders (MT), against the SRB Tribunal’s decision dated November 22, 2018. SHC determined that MT's activities constituted distribution services rather than the sale of goods, thereby subjecting MT's revenue to Sindh Sales Tax (SST) instead of Federal Sales Tax (FST). The conclusions drawn by SHC (and previously by the SRB Tribunal) were based on the contractual arrangements between MT and Colgate Palmolive (CP), which stipulated:

(i) Manufacturer appointed the distributor for specific territories/areas;
(ii) Distributor was responsible for product promotion and sales enhancement;
(iii) Distributor was obligated to maintain adequate stock levels;
(iv) Distributor was required to submit periodic stock reports to the manufacturer;
(v) Manufacturer retained the right to repurchase unsold stock from the distributor;
(vi) Distributor was bound by the manufacturer's directives regarding sales, pricing, and sales territories;
(vii) Distributor facilitated the manufacturer's sales efforts; and
(viii) The agreement between manufacturer and distributor delineated the nature of services.

3.1 The relevant excerpts from SHC's decision are attached as Annexure I to this memorandum.

SCP DECISION AND IMPLICATIONS

4. SCP's decision upholds SHC's findings, which were primarily based on the contractual elements between CP and MT. Consequently, transactions between manufacturers and distributors are construed as service arrangements, subjecting them to SST under the category of 'supply chain management or distribution (including delivery) services' [tariff heading 9845.0000]. Thus, FST does not apply as these transactions are not treated as 'sale of goods'.

The question arises: Does SCP's decision mean that all distribution agreements are now considered service arrangements?

OUR ANALYSIS

5. We believe that SCP's decision cannot be uniformly applied to all distribution arrangements. Its implications should be assessed on a case-by-case basis and limited to contracts/arrangements where the transfer of risk and rewards (i.e., title to goods) is conditional, with the manufacturer retaining control over pricing, discounts, etc. Transactions where risk and rewards are transferred without manufacturer control over the goods can still be argued to be subject to FST (rather than SST).

6. Previous disputes over the determination of 'sale of goods' versus services/agency relationships have been litigated. SCP's decision in the case of M/s.Pak Saudi Fertilizers Limited (2023 SCMR 1595) dated March 13, 2023, ruled that a transaction constituted an outright sale based on the criteria outlined in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Similar disputes were resolved by SHC in the case of M/s.Brook Bond Pakistan Limited (No.ITC No.300/2004) dated October 22, 2020, where substance prevailed over form in determining the nature of the transaction, which was treated as a sale of goods based on the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Relevant excerpts from these decisions are provided as Annexure II and III, respectively.

7. Additionally, SCP's decision (CP No.243/2011 & CP No.1136/2018) dated May 31, 2022, in the case of M/s. Pakistan Tobacco Company Limited & Khurshid Ali (Pepsi Cola Dealer) underscored that the same definition of 'sale' underlies both the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, and the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Thus, transactions where risk and rewards are outrightly transferred from seller to buyer are considered sales under both Acts. Relevant findings from this decision are attached as Annexure IV.

8. SCP's recent decision (January 26, 2024) should be applied within the context of distributor agreements akin to CP and MT's arrangement. It should not be construed as universally applicable to all distribution agreements but rather contingent upon specific contractual facts.

9. It is advisable to critically review distribution agreements to ascertain whether the transfer of risk and rewards in goods is effectively being accomplished. If agreements satisfy the criteria outlined in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, then FST applies. Conversely, if the terms indicate that goods have not been sold (due to manufacturer control), provincial tax implications may arise.

During the hearing, the Authorized Representative (AR) contended that payments to the advertising agency were initially exempt from withholding tax under clause (16A) of Part IV of the Second Schedule of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. The AR supported this claim by providing copies of the invoices issued by the advertising agency. However, it was noted that this clause was omitted through the Finance Act of 2015. Consequently, the appellant failed to deduct and deposit withholding tax as per the current provision, i.e., 1.5% of payments to advertising agencies for electronic and print media, under clause 2(ii)(c) of Division III of Part III of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

While I acknowledge the AR's argument that the supplier likely fulfilled their income tax obligations through the income tax return, making recovery from the appellant unjustified as it doesn't cause a loss to the government exchequer, I also uphold the view that default surcharge under section 205(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 should be applicable. This is in line with the DCIR's imposition of default surcharge due to the failure to collect tax on payments made to the advertising agency.

The rejection was based on the argument that the taxpayer did not meet the essential condition of "Using any process or technology that has not earlier been used in Pakistan and is so approved by the Engineering Development Board," as stipulated in section 2(27A)(iv). Consequently, the taxpayer's request for the grant of 'Greenfield Industrial Undertaking' stands declined.

5. Subsequently, the Company has initiated an appeal before the Honorable Appellate Tribunal, Karachi, challenging the rejection order dated September 2, 2022. The appeal is currently awaiting a hearing. In parallel, the Company has secured interim relief from the High Court of Sindh against the aforementioned rejection order.

6. Before the amendment by the Tax Laws (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 2021, the profits of undertakings approved by the Commissioner as 'greenfield' were exempt from tax for a period of five years under clause 126O of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance. Presently, a tax credit under section 65G of the Ordinance is available for investments in "greenfield industrial undertakings," equivalent to twenty-five percent of the "eligible investment amount." Any unadjusted tax credit not utilized in the current year can be carried forward for a period not exceeding two years.

The Finance Act of 2021 introduced significant changes to Section 12(2)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance]. Initially, the section broadly defined "salary" to encompass various allowances provided by employers, covering expenses such as cost of living, rent, education, and travel. However, it excluded allowances solely used for the employee's duties.

Recognizing potential misuse, especially in conjunction with clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule, the Act addressed this by incorporating an explanatory note into Section 12(c)(2). Simultaneously, to prevent exploitation, it omitted clause (39) from Part I of the Second Schedule.

This amendment clarifies that any allowance, irrespective of its basis or actual expenditure on behalf of the employer, will no longer qualify as an allowance for the performance of duties. The objective is to enhance transparency and ensure a fair and consistent application of tax regulations.

2. **Loss on Disposal of Fixed Assets:**
   Regarding the loss on the disposal of fixed assets, the appellant explained that they suffered a loss of Rs 3,082,332 during the tax period. The appellant received proceeds of Rs 1,039,405 against these disposals, as evidenced in the cash flow statement. The detailed breakdown of asset-wise disposals was provided, along with clarifications on specific assets. Notably, assets exempt from sales tax, as per the Sixth Schedule of the Act, were highlighted, emphasizing that the question of imposing sales tax did not arise in those cases.

The Commissioner (Appeals) found merit in the appellant's explanations and evidence, acknowledging the diligent discharge of sales tax obligations and providing a comprehensive breakdown of income and disposals. Consequently, the Commissioner (Appeals) determined that the appellant's position is valid and compliant with tax regulations.

In this context, it is important to note that prior to the Finance Act of 2021, Section 12(2)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance] defined salary to encompass various allowances provided by an employer to an employee, including those for cost of living, subsistence, rent, utilities, education, entertainment, or travel. However, it explicitly excluded allowances solely expended in the performance of the employee’s duties of employment.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned Section 12(2)(c) of the Ordinance was susceptible to misuse, particularly concerning the exemption for allowances solely expended in the performance of an employee's duty, as outlined in clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule. These provisions were exploited to evade taxes. In an effort to streamline and address this issue, an explanation has been inserted in clause (c) of sub-section (2) of Section 12 of the Ordinance. Consequently, clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule has been omitted.

Following this amendment, any allowance paid on a fixed basis, a percentage of salary, or actually spent on behalf of the employer will no longer be considered an allowance for the performance of duties.

In this context, it is imperative to provide a comprehensive understanding of the changes introduced by the Finance Act of 2021 to Section 12(2)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance]. Prior to the amendment, this section defined "salary" to include various allowances disbursed by an employer to an employee. These allowances encompassed a range of expenses such as cost of living, subsistence, rent, utilities, education, entertainment, or travel. Notably, the definition excluded allowances solely expended in the performance of the employee’s duties of employment.
Nevertheless, it became evident that the provisions of Section 12(2)(c), especially in conjunction with clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule, were susceptible to misuse. This led to an unintended exploitation of the exemption for allowances solely expended in the performance of an employee's duty, resulting in tax avoidance strategies.
To address these concerns and enhance clarity in the tax regime, an explanatory note has been incorporated into clause (c) of sub-section (2) of Section 12 of the Ordinance. Simultaneously, to streamline the process and prevent misuse, clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule has been omitted.
As a consequence of this amendment, it is crucial to note that any allowance, whether paid on a fixed basis, a percentage of salary, or not ‘actually’ spent on behalf of the employer, will no longer be categorized as an allowance for the performance of duties. This modification aims to foster transparency and ensure a fair and consistent application of tax regulations.

A plain reading of clause (i) shows that it has two distinct parts, firstly, manufacture of goods and materials and, secondly, subjection of goods or materials to any process which substantially changes, their original condition. In its wisdom the legislature has used language which clearly draws a distinction between these two parts and inevitably have to be read disjunctively. This distinction is crucial for discerning the legislative intent. Though, prima facia, they appear to be similar, but the language of the latter part has a much wider meaning and extends to eventualities beyond the conventional manufacturing of goods and materials. These two phrases cannot be treated as having the same meaning and covering similar situations, otherwise one would be rendered redundant or superfluous. The concept of taxing the income on import stage was first introduced through Finance Act, 1991, with the insertion of section 80C to the 1979 Ordinance, reproduced below for ease of reference.

“80C.	Tax on income of certain contractors and importers.- (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance or any other law for the time being in force, where any amount referred to in sub-section (2) is received by or accrues or arises or is deemed to accrue or arise to the said person and tax thereon shall be charged at the rate specified in the First Schedule.

(a)	Where the person is a resident,-

	……………………….” (emphasis ours)


This concept was retained in the 2001 Ordinance in terms of sub-section (7) of section 148 of the 2001 Ordinance, reproduced below for ease of reference.

`4“(7)	Except in the case of an industrial undertaking importing goods as raw materials [plant, machinery and equipment]1 for its own use, the tax collected under this 
section shall be final tax on the income of the importer arising from the imports subject to sub-section (1).”

Subsequently, through Finance Act, 2006, the above provisions were substituted with:

“(7)	The tax required to be collected under this section shall be a final tax except as provided under sub-section (8) on the income of the importers arising from the imports subject to sub-section (1) and this sub-section shall not apply in the case of import of-

(a)	raw material, plant and machinery, equipment and parts by an industrial undertaking for its own use; 
…………” (emphasis ours)


You would note that it is apparent from above, that the Legislature has taxed the “income of the importer” arising from imports and not the import value of the goods imported to Pakistan. “A new section namely Section 80C has been inserted in the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979, which together with paragraph CCC and the sub-stituted paragraph F of Part I of the First Schedule provides for presumptive tax for contractors, suppliers and commercial importers. 
… ………………” (emphasis ours)

"A perusal of subsection (1) of section 147 reveals that it provides that every taxpayer subject to the provisions of subsection (2) which provides that those individuals whose latest taxable income excluding the heads of income mentioned in the exclusions (a) to (d) provided in subsection (1) is Rs.500,000 or more, shall be liable to pay advance tax. Subsection (4) provides how the advance tax payable by a company or an association of persons shall be computed.

Subsection (4A) provides that the companies and association of persons shall estimate their tax payable for the relevant tax year at any time before the last installment is due and in case they find that the tax payable is likely to be more than the amount they are required to pay under the formula provided in subsection (4) then they shall furnish an estimate of the amount of the tax payable by them and thereafter pay such amount after adjustment for the amount if any already paid, in terms of subsection (4), whereas subsection (6) provides that if any taxpayer who was required to make payment of advance tax estimates before the last installment is due, that the tax payable by him for the relevant tax year is likely to the less than the amount required to be paid under subsection (1), he may furnish to the Commissioner an estimate of the amount of the tax payable by him and thereafter pay such estimated amount. A comprehensive reading of subsection (6) also leads to the conclusion that all taxpayers who are liable to pay advance tax under subsection (1), are entitled to the benefit provided, in this section and companies and association of persons have not been excluded from the benefit given to the taxpayers under this subsection. What the Assessing Officer has done is that he wants to get the benefit of the subsection (4-A) if taxpayer estimates that his tax is likely to be more than the tax payable under subsection (4) but does not want to give benefit to the corporate taxpayer if he estimates that the tax payable by him for the relevant tax year is estimated, to be less than the tax payable by him. The analysis of Section 147 reveals its applicability to taxpayers, particularly those with a taxable income of Rs.500,000 or more, excluding specified income heads. Subsection (4) outlines the computation of advance tax for companies and associations of persons. Subsection (4A) mandates companies and associations to estimate their tax liability for the tax year before the last installment, adjusting prior payments. If the estimated tax exceeds the amount calculated in subsection (4), they must pay the difference. Conversely, Subsection (6) allows taxpayers to estimate a lower tax amount than required by subsection (1) and pay the estimated sum. This provision benefits all liable taxpayers, with no exclusion for companies or associations. The Assessing Officer's approach appears biased, seeking benefits from subsection (4A) while denying corporate taxpayers similar benefits for lower estimates. Subsection (7) and Section 205 serve as deterrents for incorrect estimates under subsection (6), allowing recovery of shortfalls and imposing penalties if advance tax falls below ninety percent of the chargeable tax.

The Islamabad High Court, in a detailed judgment, overturned the Tribunal's order and clarified the interpretation of section 2(29C) of the Ordinance. The Court emphasized the distinction within clause (i), particularly in the phrases 'manufacture of goods and materials' and 'subjection of goods or materials to any process which substantially changes their original condition.' This differentiation, the Court argued, is vital to understanding the legislative intent, encompassing technological advancements beyond conventional manufacturing methods.

The High Court ruled that the subjection of goods or materials to a process, changing their original condition, extends to various scenarios beyond traditional manufacturing. The terms 'goods' and 'materials' were elucidated with reference to dictionary meanings, incorporating substances and matter from which something is made. Similarly, 'process' was defined as a series of actions, changes, or operations undergone, extending to various methods, systems, or techniques.

The judgment underscored that the expressions 'materials' and 'process' encompass a broad spectrum, including information, data, and various forms of raw materials. The Court also drew attention to Telenor Pakistan's case, establishing that even if a company provides services, it can be considered an 'industrial undertaking' under section 2(29C) if it meets the criteria outlined in clause (i).

The court highlighted the significance of considering factual aspects, such as the nature of imported goods, their use by the company, and the processes involved in substantially changing the form of raw materials. The decision rejected a rigid interpretation, emphasizing the broader scope of 'material' and 'process.'

In the context of tax implications, the argument was presented that considering tax paid on imported plant and machinery as non-advance tax would not only contradict legislative intent but also disrupt tax collection. The historical evolution of tax provisions, specifically section 148(7), was explained, demonstrating that the taxation focus is on the income of the importer arising from imports rather than the import value.

Furthermore, the concept of "commercial importer" was acknowledged through Circular No. 12 of 1991, affirming the applicability of the presumptive tax scheme to commercial importers under section 80C of the repealed Income Tax Ordinance, 1979.

In conclusion, the arguments emphasized the need for a nuanced understanding of the legislative framework, recognizing the evolving nature of technology and the expansive scope of terms like 'materials' and 'process' in determining the status of a company as an 'industrial undertaking' under section 2(29C) of the Ordinance.

Prior to the amendment, this section defined "salary" to include various allowances disbursed by an employer to an employee. These allowances encompassed a range of expenses such as cost of living, subsistence, rent, utilities, education, entertainment, or travel. Notably, the definition excluded allowances solely expended in the performance of the employee’s duties of employment.

However, it became evident that the provisions of Section 12(2)(c), especially in conjunction with clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule, were susceptible to misuse. This led to an unintended exploitation of the exemption for allowances solely expended in the performance of an employee's duty, resulting in tax avoidance strategies.

To address these concerns and enhance clarity in the tax regime, an explanatory note has been incorporated into clause (c) of sub-section (2) of Section 12 of the Ordinance. Simultaneously, to streamline the process and prevent misuse, clause (39) of Part I of the Second Schedule has been omitted.

As a consequence of this amendment, it is crucial to note that any allowance, whether paid on a fixed basis, a percentage of salary, or actually spent on behalf of the employer, will no longer be categorized as an allowance for the performance of duties. This modification aims to foster transparency and ensure a fair and consistent application of tax regulations.

Dear Muhammad Faraz,

I hope this message finds you well. Thank you for reaching out to us regarding the taxation of the intended payment of a golden handshake from Shell Pakistan Limited. Based on our understanding, you are currently a non-resident individual working at Qatar Shell GTL Limited as an Aviation Operations Lead. Kindly confirm this understanding.

I would like to highlight that any salary received by an individual for employment in Pakistan is considered Pakistan-source income. Conversely, any amount received for employment conducted outside Pakistan is regarded as foreign-source income, regardless of where it is paid.

Therefore, the portion of your salary or termination benefits attributable to employment exercised in Pakistan will be subject to Pakistani taxation. However, the salary allocated to workdays outside Pakistan will not be taxable in Pakistan as it constitutes foreign-source income for a non-resident individual.

If a Pakistani citizen leaves the country during a tax year and remains abroad for the entire year, any salary earned outside Pakistan during that period is exempt from Pakistani taxation, especially during the relocation or transitionary period.

It's important to note that the employer should only withhold tax from the portion of the salary under Section 149 of the Ordinance that is taxable in Pakistan. The portion that is not taxable under Pakistani law should not be subject to withholding tax. The employee may then claim credit under the double tax treaty in their country of residence for any tax deducted in Pakistan.

Based on the above discussion, I suggest requesting your employer to bifurcate the benefits received between the employment exercised in Pakistan and outside Pakistan. Only the portion related to employment in Pakistan should be considered taxable under Section 149 of the Ordinance.

Please feel free to reach out if you need any further clarification or assistance.

Consequently, starting from July 1, 2018, SPL is obligated to apply the full Punjab sales tax rate of sixteen percent on franchise services.

Now, with regard to Rule 10 of the Punjab Sales Tax on Services (Adjustment of Tax) Rules, 2012, it grants services providers the flexibility to issue a supplementary tax invoice when there is a need to modify the value of services and the amount of tax specified in the original invoice on the higher side. This provision is applicable in our current situation, where adjustments are required.

Allow me to reproduce Rule 10 for your reference:

"10. Supplementary tax invoice: Where, for any reason, the value of service and the amount of tax mentioned on the tax invoice are required to be modified on the higher side, the registered person providing service may issue a supplementary tax invoice mentioning particulars of the principal invoice and account for the same in the return of the tax period during which the supplementary invoice is issued."

It's crucial to emphasize that, as per the rule, the supplementary invoice should be declared in the same tax period in which it is issued.

However, anticipating potential concerns from the tax department, it's worth noting that there might be a dispute regarding the interpretation of the conditions under which a supplementary tax invoice can be issued. The tax department may argue that it is permissible only when the amount of tax changes on the higher side. Nevertheless, in the event of such a dispute, we have a reasonable argument to assert that both conditions—namely, a change in the value of services and the amount of tax mentioned on the tax invoice on the higher side—can be considered independently. To clarify, a supplementary invoice can only be issued when there is a change in one condition, specifically, the tax mentioned on the tax invoice on the higher side, which aligns with our current scenario.

Hi Komal,

I trust this message finds you well. Regarding the default surcharge implications, we would like to bring to your attention the existing conflicting decisions from appellate authorities, with perspectives favoring both the taxpayer and the tax department.

Primarily, the central contention raised by the AR of taxpayers revolves around the inclusion of the mens rea element. According to this argument, in the absence of mens rea, the imposition of default surcharge and penalty becomes unwarranted. However, it's noteworthy that a recent decision by the honorable Lahore High Court (LHC) ruled in favor of the tax department, even in cases where no tax liability exists.

The specific legal question before the LHC was whether the Tribunal's decision, influenced by a prior judgment in the case vide No. STA 262/KB/2018, was justified in asserting that Section 11(1) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 [STA], does not permit the imposition of default surcharge and penalty under Sections 34 and 33, respectively. The Tribunal's reasoning was based on the scenario where the taxpayer had only settled the principal amount of sales tax before the issuance of notice under section 11(1).

LHC opined that the decision of the Bench of High Court (BHC) had a restrictive interpretation that could potentially undermine the disciplined compliance envisioned in the law, rendering Sections 33 and 34 redundant. The court further noted that the BHC's decision failed to consider prior judgments, such as in the cases of Madina Cotton Ginners and Oil Mills (2016 PTD 643) and Messrs Attack Refinery Limited.

The legal questions were resolved in favor of the Tax Department, with LHC asserting that the Tribunal's order was legally defective. However, the matter has been remitted to the Appellate Tribunal for de novo determination.

In light of the above, safeguarding against default surcharge and penalty at the higher appellate forum is grounded in the justification of the absence of mens rea. We acknowledge that establishing the absence of mens rea in this instance may pose challenges, especially given that the deposit of the principal amount was not voluntary from your side. Hi Komal,

Indeed, your understanding is accurate; the reduced-rate notification was extended until June 2018. Consequently, starting July 1, 2018, SPL is obligated to discharge Punjab sales tax on franchise services at the full rate, i.e., sixteen percent.

Additionally, in accordance with Rule 10 of the Punjab Sales Tax on Services (Adjustment of Tax) Rules, 2012, a services provider has the provision to issue a supplementary tax invoice for any reason requiring a modification to the value of services and the amount of tax stated in the original invoice on the higher side, as is the case here. It's essential to note that this supplementary invoice should be declared in the same tax period in which it is issued. For brevity, Rule 10 of the Punjab Sales Tax on Services (Adjustment of Tax) Rules, 2012 is reproduced below:

"10. Supplementary tax invoice: Where, for any reason, the value of service and the amount of tax mentioned on the tax invoice are required to be modified on the higher side, the registered person providing service may issue a supplementary tax invoice mentioning particulars of the principal invoice and account for the same in the return of the tax period during which the supplementary invoice is issued."

It's important to acknowledge that the tax department may contest the issuance of a supplementary tax invoice, arguing that it should only be done when the amount of tax changes on the higher side. However, in the event of a dispute, we have a reasonable argument to assert that both conditions—change in the value of services and the amount of tax mentioned on the tax invoice on the higher side—can be interpreted separately. In other words, a supplementary invoice can only be issued when there is a change in one condition, namely, the tax mentioned on the tax invoice on the higher side, as is the situation in our case.

Addressing the loss incurred on the disposal of fixed assets amounting to Rs 3,082,332, the AR provided a comprehensive explanation during the hearing. The appellant had suffered losses from the disposal of various assets and proceeds of Rs 1,039,405 were received and duly reflected in the cash flow statement under "Proceeds from disposal of property, plant and equipment." The AR further presented an asset-wise detailed breakdown, emphasizing assets that were scrapped or entitled to employees, where no proceeds were received, and thus, no sales tax discharge was applicable. Importantly, assets exempt from sales tax under the Sixth Schedule of the Act were highlighted, supported by a sound legal argument based on Section 8(1)(i) of the Act, which restricts input tax claims against vehicle purchases. 

I have heard the arguments, perused the record, given earnest consideration to the arguments and have keenly gone through the material relied upon by the AR and perused the impugned order. I am inclined towards the arguments taken by the learned AR on behalf of the appellant for the reasons discussed below. The Honorable Supreme Court in a case reported as 96 Tax 105 reached a conclusion that even if the supplier of goods (fixed assets) is not in the business of such goods but the sales proceeds therefrom are utilized in its business, then such proceeds would qualify to be in the course of or furtherance of taxable activity and, thus, would be chargeable to sales tax under section 3(1 )(a) of the ST Act. Nevertheless, such conclusion was based on the law as it existed in the year 1996 and the subsequent amendments therein were not taken into account, a fact recorded in paragraph 13 of the said judgement:

"13. In order to appreciate the divergent arguments , advanced by the learned counsel for the parties, which mainly relate to controversy over the interpretation of the different provisions of the Sales Tax Act, it may be advantageous to reproduce the relevant sections and the expression/terms and words used both in the Act and after its amendment in the year 1996 through Finance Act, 1996 as the aforesaid provisions cover the sales tax period involved in the instant cases. However subsequently some other amendments were also made but those are not relevant for the purpose of deciding the present cases."


The definition of term 'taxable supply', contained in section 2(41) of the ST Act, underwent certain amendments through Finance Act, 1998. Both the said definitions, i.e., prior to amendments made through Finance Act, 1998 and the provisions as enacted pursuant to these amendments are reproduced below:

Pre-amended

"taxable supply" means a supply of taxable goods made other than a supply ofgoods which is exempt under section 13 and includes a supply of goods chargeable to tax at the rate of zero per cent under section 4.

Post-amended

"taxable supply" means a supply of taxable goods made by an importer, manufacturer, wholesaler · (including dealer). distributor or retailer other than a supply of goods which is exempt under section 13 and includes a supply of goods chargeable to tax at the rate of zero per cent under section 4. (emphasis added)


Upon comparison of both these definitions, it readily emerges that, pursuant to amendments made through Finance Act, 1998, the definition of 'taxable supply' was restricted to include only such supplies which were made by importer, manufacturer, wholesaler (including dealer), distributor or retailer. It is an undisputed fact that the appellant does not fall into any of the said five categories of suppliers. Thus, I am of the candid view that the imposition of sales tax was not applicable in this specific case. 

Without prejudice to our above findings if for an arguments sake, it is assumed that the above-referred judgment of the Supreme Court is relevant in the instant case, even then the same does not come to the rescue of the department. It is an undeniable fact as already upheld by the honourable Sindh High Court· through judgement reported as 2017 PTD 1, that after the 18th Amendment to the Constitution, which took effect on 19-10-2010, the right to impose indirect tax on services got devolved to Provinces. There is no cavil to the facts that the principal 'taxable activity' of the appellant falls under the domain of provincial authorities for the purposes of levying any sales tax. The DCIR failed to note that when the 'taxable activity' is not a Federal subject in the first place, then any 'furtherance' thereto can obviously not be subjected to Federal sales tax either. Even the honourable Supreme Court, in the judgment referred supra, has held that 'taxable activity' and 'furtherance' thereto are not to be read in isolation, rather both these terms are inter-related. Relevant portion of the said judgment is reproduced below:

"24.. . . These goods were purchased by the respondents in the course of their taxable activity, their sale cannot be considered as a transaction which is divorced from their normal business and that the said goods are business assets of the respondent and both their purchase and sale is a part of their normal business activity."


I also find strength by the following findings of the honourable Lahore High Court in the case titled as Commissioner Inland Revenue versus M/s Golden Pearl Cosmetics reported as 2017 PTD 1485, holding in categorical and unequivocal terms that, after the 18th Amendment to the Constitution, the provisions of the ST Act imposing sales tax on services stand repealed impliedly:

“15. ... This has created an anomalous situation because on one hand, the Rules of 2007 levy Federal sales tax on advertisement services and on the other hand, Act of 2012 and rules there underalso levy provincial sales tax on · the same advertisement services. This situation squarely attracts well established maxim leges "posteriors prior escontrariasabrogant" means later laws repeal earlier law inconsistent therewith. It is settled law that in case of conflict between two laws, preference would be given to the new law and implied repeal of earlier law would be inferred where enactment of later law is totally inconsistent with the earlier law. In normal circumstances, the Federal Law will prevail over Provincial Law but in the present scenario, after the 18th Amendment, the legislative competence to enact law regarding services being with the Province, the Provincial Act of 2012 will prevail over subsection (3A) of section 2 of Rules 2007. 

16. The essential condition for implied repeal is that when provision of former statute is inconsistent and in conflict with the provision of later statute and the two cannot be reconciled or harmonized, so as to stand together. In such situation the provision of earlier statute will give way to similar provision in the later statute on the basis of doctrine of implied repeal. ... No doubt under sub-Articles (6) and (7) of Article 270AA of the Constitution, the rule 2(3A) of · the Rules of 2007 were to remain in force until repeal, however, as discussed above, the said rule has been impliedly repealed after Act of 2012.

17. In the given circumstances, after promulgation of Act of 2012, and issuance of notification under section 1(4) of the said Act regarding levy of Provincial sales tax inter alia on advertisement services, the earlier provision of sub-rule (3A) of rule 2 of Rules 2007, levying withholding of sales tax on same advertisement serves, will deemed to be impliedly repealed...


Accordingly, on this tangent too, I am convinced that the DCIR had erred materially by applying incorrect law and charging Federal sales tax in the instant case. I also find merits with arguments of the learned AR that not charging Federal sales tax in the instant case. The appeal is hereby, accepted and in the light of the above submissions and documents furnished by the AR. I do not find any merit in the findings of the DCIR given in the impugned order. Resultantly, the demand worked against the appellant through the impugned order stands deleted.

10. Supplementary tax invoice:– Where for any reason, the value of service and amount of tax mentioned on the tax invoice are required to be modified on higher side, the registered person providing service may, issue a supplementary tax invoice mentioning particulars of the principal invoice and account for the same in the return of the tax period during which supplementary invoice is issued.
It is pertinent to mention here that the tax department might dispute it that existence of both conditions i.e., value of services and amount of tax mentioned in the invoice would require to change on higher side then a service provider issue a supplementary tax invoice only in the circumstance when only amount of tax change of the high side. It appears from the impugned order that there was no reason assigned that as to how and what documents were lacking in details / documents admittedly filed by the appellant. The officer stated that input claims were rejected that the material/purchases made are not directly related in the manufacturing process and stands inadmissible. 

Such disallowance in perfunctory manner cannot be held to be justified as Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan has time and again unapproved the passing of such perfunctory orders in the cases involving valuable rights of the parties. It is settled law that quasi-judicial order must be a speaking order manifesting by itself that the forum has applied its judicial mind in the cases as if the reasons would not be forthcoming, obviously the appellate court would be deprived of the views of the subordinate forum. 

It also appears that the officer did apply the mind at broader level using legal provisions whilst ignoring the factual aspects of the case. Infect, when these purchases relates to items consumed in business activities and there is no dispute that all supplies of the appellant are taxable, question of disqualification in term of SRO 490 does not arise at the outset. For disallowing any claim of input tax, the officer needs to identify the factual aspects besides using the legal provisions. Disallowance under specific provision should be supported by factual aspect as well. In view of that I totally agree with the appellant that details were submitted. I am also quite convinced form the judgements of the M/s Chashma Sugar Mills wherein it has been held that section 8 cannot override section 7 of the Act.

While acceding to the submissions of learned AR, I also derive strength from the most recent Judgement of Honorable ATIR Karachi Bench in case of Khaipur Sugar Mills vs. CIR STA No. 426/KB/2017 pronounced on 05.04.2018. The operative part of the said judgement is reproduced as under:

“11.	We have perused the impugned orders of the below authorities and have gone through the records available and have also considered the judgments of Courts on the issue. It is not disputed that the appellant is a manufacturer or white crystalline sugar and claimed input tax adjustments on goods and services purchased / rendered with valid sales tax invoices and used the same within the business premises of the mills for manufacturing of taxable activity, veracity of which has not been questioned. Thus there has been created a legitimate right of input tax adjustment or refund under the provisions of section 7 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 for the appellant. However, the officer denied input tax adjustment to the appellant in terms of section 8(1)(a) without any reasoning or evidence that the alleged goods were used for the purpose other than for taxable supplies and held that the adjustment made by the appellant is in violation of section 8(1)(a), (c) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Before any conclusion is drawn, it is imperative to reproduce section (1)(a), (c) and (h) as the same is relevant for the sake of brevity:

	“8(1)(a) --- the goods [or services] used or to be used for any purpose other than for taxable supplies made or to be made by him;]

	(c) [***] the goods under 12 [sub-section] (5) of section 3 13[:]

	(h)---Goods used in, or permanently attached to, immoveable property, such as building and construction materials, paints, electrical and sanitary fittings, pipes, wires and cables, but excluding such goods acquired for sale or re-sale or for direct use in the production or manufacture of taxable goods; and 

12.	On perusal of section 8(1)(a), it is abundantly clear that those goods or services which are used for any purpose other than taxable supplies are not reclaimable. In this case of the appellant the officer has failed to establish this crucial aspect of case, whether the appellant’s goods were used for any purpose other than taxable supply. Rather on perusal of impugned order-in-original, it is found that the officer has himself admitted that the purchased items have been used by the appellant for manufacturing of taxable goods but the same are not the integral part of taxable supplies. As the appellant produces white crystalline sugar which is a taxable supply, hence any input goods which are solely used for obtaining taxable supply shall be available for adjustment to the appellant. We fully agree with the reported judgment of Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan PTCL 2017 CL-217 which undoubtedly makes it clear that the provision of section 8(1)(a) can only be invoked where supplies made by a taxpayer are exempt.”

14	Further, on perusal of clause (h) of section 8, it is found that certain items are not available for input tax adjustment unless they are used in manufacturing of taxable goods. As just stated above the appellant is engaged in the manufacturing of while crystalline sugar and molasses which are taxable goods therefore any taxable purchases which are solely used within the business premises of the appellant for the manufacturing of taxable goods are available for adjustment. We have perused the reported judgement PTD 2014 CL-558 copy of which was provided by A/R wherein it has been held as under.

”Goods ” in the present case, were not used for any purpose other than taxable supplies provision of section 8(1)(a) of the Sales tax Act 1990 were not attracted nor the entitlement of input tax thereon was precluded by a notification under section 8(1)(a) of the Sales tax Act 1990 ---Denial from input tax adjustment or the credit paid on such goods was illegal and unlawful and violation of mandatory provisions law---No condition of direct relation of input goods to manufacturing of finished goods was provided in section 8(1)(a) of the Sales tax Act 1990, however condition of its use for the purpose of making of taxable supplies was specified therein and the taxpayer do qualify for entitlement of input tax credit on the goods in question as the same were not used for any purpose other than for taxable supplies because all of the supplies made taxpayer was not well versed with the use of kerosene oil which was used for the purpose of making pulp from raw materials like straw, husk and raddi, etc. Which was used for making of paper and paper board products ---Since, kerosene was wholly used for the purpose of taxable supplies only no recovery could be made from the taxpayer.

15.	We also refer to a reported judgement 2012 PTCL 475 copy of which was by the A/R where in it has been as under.

“In the case we have no hesitation in our minds that chilling equipment was not used for any purpose other than for taxable supplies made or to be made by the appellant. The provisions of law authorize deduction for all such input tax that relates to goods that contribute directly or indirectly and even remotely towards furtherance of taxable activity. In the case we observe that it is not at all disputed that subject chilling equipment is being used to chill the beverage products supplied by the appellant and hence, any denial of input tax adjustment is not understandable. Clearly the connection/nexus of chilling equipment with appellant ’s business is established which is also admitted by the adjudicating officer in one of order in originals assailed in these appeals wherein he observed that the respondent supplied these equipments to their dealers for facilitating the sales and for publicity of their product. In the presence of such observation, we are at loss to understand as to how department is contending for disallowance of related adjustment of input tax. For all intent and purpose the subject goods were for the purposes of taxable supplies of the appellant and hence were not hit by the mischief of provisions of section 8(1)(a) of the Act. The expression purpose has a very wife application and according to dictionary meaning the same refers to what something is supposed to be achieved. In this case there is no doubt that chilling equipment as placed to achieve growth in the business and that fulfills the requirement of purpose as used in the relevant provisions of law.”

16. Hi Komal, we respect the default surcharge implication, we would inform you that there are conflicting decisions available from appellate authorities both in favor of the taxpayer and tax department. Nevertheless, the principal / main contention for the AR of the taxpayers in the involvement of mens rea element. In the absence of the mens rea, default surcharge and penalty cannot be imposed. However, recently, the honorable Lahore High Court (LHC) decided the matter of imposition of default surcharge and penalty in favor of the tax department even in the case of no tax is payable. 

Question of law before LHC is to whether Tribunal was justified to hold, while placing its reliance on Tribunal's judgement in case vide No. STA 262/KB/2018, that Section 11(1) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 [STA] do not allow the imposition of default surcharge and penalty under Sections 34 and 33, respectively, where taxpayer has only discharged principal amount of sales tax before issuance of notice under section 11(1).    

LHC found that BHC's decision has Restrictive interpretation that would nullifies the disciplined compliance envisaged in law and otherwise render sections 33 and 34, redundant. Also, LHC noted that BHC's decision has not appreciated earlier decisions made in the cases like Madina Cotton Ginners and Oil MIIIs (2016 PTD 643) and Messrs Attack Refinery Limited.

The said questions of laws have been decided in favor Tax Department and LHC ordered that Tribunal's order is legally defective. However, the matter was remitted to Appellate Tribunal for de nova determination.

Keeping in view of the above, safeguarding default surcharge and penalty from the higher appellate forum is the justification of no element of mens rea. Nevertheless, we understand that justification of no element of mens rea in the instant case would be difficult task because the said deposit of principle amount is not voluntary from your side. But it was highlight by the tax department through informal communication.

Subject: Clarification on Issuance of Credit Notes for Change of Invoice Date

Hi Danish,

I trust this message finds you well.

In response to your email dated December 1, 2023, seeking our opinion on the issuance of credit notes due to a change in the invoice date with the same taxable value and sales tax, I would like to provide the following insights.

As per our understanding, the construction invoices dated June 29, 2022, and August 29, 2022, related to Punjab sales tax, with the respective sales tax amounts duly deposited to the Punjab Revenue Authority, and payments for the invoices have already been made by TGDC. The request now is to change the invoice dates to any month in the year 2023 while maintaining the same values.

Upon reviewing the situation, it is crucial to assess whether the provisions of the Punjab Sales Tax on Services Act, 2012, permit the alteration of the invoice date alone. Rule 8 of the Punjab Sales Tax on Services (Adjustment of Tax) Rules, 2012, outlines that a registered person can issue a credit note to adjust the amount shown in the tax invoice on the lower side due to any genuine business reason within ninety days of the tax period in which such modification is required.

In the context of the current scenario, and considering the stipulations of the mentioned rule, changing the date of the invoice is not permissible under the law. The taxpayer is allowed to adjust the amount shown in the tax invoice through a debit or credit note, but it's important to note that the specified timeline for issuing such notes has already lapsed.

I trust these clarifications address your inquiry. Should you have any further questions or concerns, please feel free to reach out for additional assistance.

This payment is made in connection with the allotment of land to operate and maintain the container terminal based on containers handled at the Terminal maintained by FOTCO, spanning a thirty-year period.

Additionally, PQA undertakes key functions to facilitate terminal operations on the allotted land:

Therefore, the payment could potentially be classified either as rent for the lease of land, considering that a significant portion of the total payment pertains to the right to use the land. Alternatively, it could be seen as payment for services provided by PQA to facilitate terminal operations. A detailed analysis of the benefits received by FOTCO against the payment recognized as "Royalty" in the books of accounts would be necessary, as substance takes precedence over nomenclature.

It's worth noting that some terminal operators have consistently maintained that this payment is for land use rather than for services rendered.

In conclusion, the company may adopt a position with provincial sales authorities that the payment to PQA is for the use of land, emphasizing that, despite being labeled as royalty in the Implementation Agreements, it does not involve the provision of services.

Considering the above, we suggest that tax be deducted under section 155 of the Ordinance at the applicable rate of 15%.

We refer to your email through which you sought our opinion regarding charged created in the books on account of SWPPF. In this regard, we would inform you that the contribution under SWPPF Act is payable at the rate of 5 per cent of profits by companies engaged in industrial undertakings which satisfies any one of the prescribed criteria relating to minimum share capital, fixed assets and workers. The definition of ‘profit’ under SWPPF Act is given as “profits" in relation to a company means such of the "net profits" as are attributable in its business, trade, undertakings or other operations in Pakistan". The terms “business, trade, undertaking, and other operations” have not been defined under the SWPPF Act. 

In the absence of the definitions under the legislation, the superior courts have generally settled a principle that if a legislation does not provide a specific definition for a term, their dictionary meaning should be taken for the purpose of drawing a conclusion in this regard. The ordinary meaning of the terms ‘business’ and ‘trade’ are very wide to cover any conceivable activity carried on for profit. The term ‘undertaking’ is controlled by the terms ‘business’ and ‘trade’ and therefore analogous to these terms. The term ‘other operations’ appears to be a general term, so therefore this also refers to activities similar to business, trade and undertaking.


Furthermore, the phrase "as are attributable to" manifestly signifies that "all" the profits are not envisaged, to be taken into consideration and there are certain profits, that are deliberately, and patently intended to be left out. Furthermore, the Scheme of WPPF is applicable only to companies engaged in an industrial undertaking. It means companies, not engaged in industrial undertaking, are not subject to the Scheme, although such companies fulfil other conditions of its applicability being either number of employees, paid-up capital or fixed assets etc. This leads to another argument that the net profits of the company as are attributable to its business, trade, undertaking or other operations in Pakistan, needs to be considered in the light of company’s operations pertaining to the industrial undertaking in which the company is engaged excluding its other activity which doesnot pertain to the industrial undertakings. 

Having said that, it is important to note that the Sindh WPPF Act is a relatively new legislation, and it has yet to be seen as to how the courts will interpret the law about matter under discussion. When Civil Appeal No. 51 of 2020, order wherein is assailed herein, was heard it was contended that the order amending the assessment was passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Inland Revenue, who was not authorized to amend the assessment. At that time, we were also assisted by Mr. Sohail Ahmed, Additional Commissioner, Regional Tax Office, Peshawar and neither he nor the learned ASC could produce any delegation of authority by the Commissioner of his said powers to the Deputy Commissioner despite grant of a further opportunity to do so (as noted in paragraph 3 of the order under review).

2.	The order of this Court is now sought to be reviewed on the ground that the Deputy Commissioner was delegated powers to amend the assessment vide order No. 616, dated 5 December 2009, issued by the Commissioner Inland Revenue (Audit-I), Regional Tax Office, Peshawar (‘the said order’) mentioned at serial No. 1 of the Table contained in the said order.

3.	However, the said order does not refer to section 122 of the Ordinance with regard to amendment of assessment nor is it so stated under column No. 4 of the Table pertaining to Jurisdiction.

4.	We enquired from the learned counsel whether the said order has been gazette and were informed that it was not. We then enquired whether that said order is available on the website of the Federal Board of Revenue (‘FBR’) and were told that it was not. It is beyond comprehension why this has not been disclosed. Surely the reason for concealment could not be to use it in appropriate cases and suppress it in others. Nonetheless opaqueness perturbs us. Taxpayers should know who is exercising authority and whether such exercise of authority is permissible.

5.	This civil review petition is a classic example of a case not properly presented. The point raised today had already been argued at the time of hearing the appeal and indulgence had also been shown to the petitioner (Commissioner Inland Revenue) to disclose the requisite authority bestowed on the Deputy Commissioner. Dear Anas,

I am pleased to share some positive news with you regarding the recent developments in your tax-related matters. The Commissioner Inland Revenue (Appeals) [CIR(A)] has successfully concluded the remand back proceedings for the tax years 2018 to 2020 in your favor.

For your convenience, I have attached the CIR(A) orders, all dated January 18, 2024, related to these proceedings. This positive outcome comes after the matter was remanded back by the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue through Order No. ITA No. 2494/KB/2023 to 2496/KB/2023, all dated October 30, 2023. This remand was in response to the Appellate Orders, all dated August 29, 2023.

The crux of the issue revolved around the rejection of the Group Return filed under section 59AA of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 [Ordinance], which included your wholly-owned subsidiary. The rejection led to the taxation of Intercorporate Dividend claimed as exempt under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance.

The grounds for rejection included your alleged failure to comply with corporate governance requirements specified by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) and the perceived ineligibility to form a group with an entity whose profits are tax-exempt. Furthermore, the ACIR incorrectly assumed the power to reject the "irrevocable" Group option and taxed the dividend income claimed exempt.

During the appeals hearing, we effectively argued that the ACIR lacks the authority to reject the Group Option once exercised, emphasizing that no objections were raised by the department when the option was initially exercised. Additionally, we highlighted that the SECP has the sole authority to disintegrate groups formed under its regulations.

We also contested the application of section 109(1)(a) and (b), asserting that the formation of the group was a necessary business exigency rather than a tax avoidance scheme. Legal precedents were cited to differentiate between tax mitigation and tax avoidance.

Fortunately, the CIR(A) accepted our contentions, particularly the valid points challenging the ACIR's authority and disputing the characterization of your actions as a tax avoidance scheme. The CIR(A) has directed the ACIR to reevaluate the case and frame a speaking order, considering specific questions raised during the hearing. For brevity, the key questions are as follows:

1. Identification of the underlying transaction recharacterized in this case and whether the declaration as a Group under section 59AA of the Ordinance qualifies as a ‘transaction’ when declared by a regulatory authority.
2. Jurisdiction for an action under section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance in the absence of a transaction.
3. Jurisdiction to declare the claim of “exemption under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule” as a “tax avoidance scheme” under section 109(2) of the Ordinance.
4. Jurisdiction under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance to disregard a Group Return filed under section 59AA upon exercise of the option after SECP approval.
5. SECP's actions during the period in question for any non-compliance with regulations, including Corporate Governance Regulations, and the applicable provision of the law that could be invoked by the Officer in case of default.

Given the remand back with specific directions, we have the option to file appeals before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue. The last date to file an appeal is March 18, 2024.

Subject: Opinion on Applicability of Sindh Sales Tax on Renting of Immovable Properties

Hi Komal,

I hope this email finds you well. Regarding your inquiry on the applicability of Sindh Sales Tax (SST) on the renting of immovable properties post the recent decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan dated September 5, 2022, I would like to provide the following analysis:

The Supreme Court's judgment confirmed the earlier decision of the Sindh High Court (SHC) in the case of Young's (Private) Limited. However, it's essential to note that the definition of "economic activity" in section 4 of the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act was amended through the Sindh Sales Tax on Services (Amendment) Act, 2018, with retrospective effect from July 1, 2015. This amendment included renting of immovable property within the purview of economic activity.

While the Supreme Court confirmed the SHC's judgment, which held that the mere renting out of property by a landlord to a tenant is not a taxable service, it's crucial to distinguish between the pre-amendment and post-amendment eras. The first part of the judgment may be argued as dependent upon the un-amended definition of economic activity, which effectively forms part of the definition of taxable service. Therefore, this part of the judgment may not be squarely applicable in the post-amended era.

However, the second part of the judgment, where the Supreme Court agreed with the SHC's view that renting of immovable property is not a "service," is based on the general connotation of the term "services" and remains unaffected by any legislative amendment. Hence, this interpretation could be applied even after the amendment of 2018.

In light of the above, our view is that the Supreme Court's decision would be applicable post the amendment Act of 2018, and consequently, SST can be argued as not applicable to the renting of immovable property.

It's important to mention that after the amendment Act of 2018, when the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) approached taxpayers asserting that SST is applicable to renting of immovable property, tenants and landlords challenged it in the SHC and obtained interim stay orders. In cases where there is no stay order from the High Court, the Bank, being a withholding agent, may either withhold sales tax or obtain an undertaking from the landlord, holding them responsible for the SST liability if SRB approaches them for non-withholding of SST.

As the matter also involves the interpretation of the Supreme Court's judgment, it is advisable for the Bank to seek the opinion of its legal counsel on this matter.
