“(8) In case, there is divestment of a subsidiary company and the provisions of group taxation become inapplicable, no effect shall be taken for group taxation during the year of disposal.”


54.	Next ,I have also carefully considered the provisions for invoking and application of section 109 (1)(a) and (b) which lay down that transactions need to be undertaken to avoid the tax due as well as the interpretation of the Sindh High Court in the case reported as 2018 PTD 114 as well as in ITA No. 723/KB/2018 reported (2022) 125 Tax 132 (Trib.) where this the matter of “tax avoidance and section 109 is discussed in detail as quoted below:

“18.	It is manifestly clear that no hard and fast rules or principles could be laid down where a provision of law is required to be construed purposively. Each and every case needs to be considered on its own facts and circumstance. The qualification and disqualification would always remain dependent on facts and circumstances of each case. We now proceed with applying the above authoritatively, unambiguously and unequivocally settled principles on the facts of the present case. In this regard, it would be in the fitness of things if the contentions of the authorities below as recorded in their respective orders, and reproduced above, are also kept in consideration. In the present case, it is patently clear that the transfer· of assets was necessitated owing to certain very pertinent business reasons. All documents on record, including, intimations to regulatory authorities and shareholders loudly and clearly depicted the underlying main purpose and objective of the complete transactions i.e., proceeding with inclusion of a joint venture partner well before the actual transaction affecting transfer of assets. As is evident from the amendment order and other assessment records, appellant has made strategic investments in various projects and in certain cases also engaged foreign partners in various business ventures. The primary purpose of subject transfer was also predominantly to bring foreign investment & foreign expertise in one of the lines of appellant's business i.e., Paper & Board and Corrugated business and for this reason, existing business was restructured by way of hive down of relevant assets into BSPL with subsequent induction of a Joint Venture partner (i.e., Stora Enso) therein. Thus, we fully concur with the learned AR's View that the overarching purpose of the transaction was nothing but business/economic consideration ultimately aimed at enrichment of business and shareholder value and was not meant wholly and exclusively for avoidance of any tax, as has been asserted by department. while the department has tried to make out a case that the series of events i.e., from the date of announcement of transfer of assets to BSPL till issuance of equity to Stora enso, constituted ‘pre-ordinated transactions’ aimed at avoidance of tax in terms of the judgements of UK jurisdiction, if has relied to appreciate the position that it is a considered view of Courts that only such transaction can attract GAAR application, whose main objective is avoidance of tax, which we have no doubts in our minds, is not the case here. The claim of tax neutrality under section 97 of the Ordinance it is apt to be noted, was only, at best, 'incidental' to achievement of appellant's main business purpose. Accordingly, in terms of ratio decidendi of the order of the Sindh High Court this transaction, holistically speaking, is not hit by the mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance.

19.	The assertion of revenue that in a series of transactions where any one individual transaction results into non imposition of tax otherwise leviable under the statute, mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance is fully applicable is, in our view, not only seriously flawed but also offends the principles settled by their lordships in order of Sindh High Court referred supra. If this was considered to be permissible, or for that matter, intent of legislature then practically all provisions extending any benefit, incentive, advantage etc. would become meaningless and redundant. Every such claim could then be disputed on notions and hypothesis. In terms of scheme envisaged in the statute benefits/concessions stipulated in sections 95, 96, 97, 97A or for that matter under sections 59AA or 59B of the Ordinance, cannot be denied without undertaking complete analysis through a purposive approach, as eloquently deliberated in the judgement cited supra. To elaborate, every action by taxpayers to undertake business re-organizations or to make them eligible for any tax mitigation / concessions etc, could not be, per se, dragged in the provisions of section 109 of the Ordinance, unit, and unless the analysis of facts/circumstances & underlying objectives indicate that principal purpose thereof is tax avoidance. If this process could be allowed to be bypassed or short circuited, the ultimate result would be that the entire super structure of law setting out benefits and advantages etc. could crumble. This, we consider, is obviously neither the  legislative intent nor a purposive interpretation of the statutory provisions. It is in this background that it is a considered view of Court that ‘tax mitigation’ and ‘tax avoidance’ need to be necessarily differentiated whilst applying the GAAR provisions and it is only in case of the latter that these come into play and that too in circumstances where the primary purpose of executing the transaction, and not the incidental purpose is 'tax avoidance'. The entire edifice built by revenue while invoking provisions of section 109 of the Ordinance in the present case is self-contradictory when at one hand the department treats transfer under section 97 of the Ordinance as hit by the mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance and in the same breath concedes that the transaction would have been tax neutral had the objective of transaction been achieved under section 97 A of the Ordinance. It is not understandable as to how, according to revenue, invocation of section 97 A of the Ordinance would have cleared the transaction from the scope of section 109 of the Ordinance when the ultimate objective of transfer of assets had stood at par as is under current circumstances.”


55.	The concluding paragraphs from the Order are as under:

“…….. However, in our opinion, under the facts of the case, this conclusion is unsafe, when there is evidence available of the fact that though the agreement to transfer assets of 15th September, 2012 was made merely two months prior to the Joint venture agreement of 15th November, 2012, however, the original decision to transfer the assets was made by the PL in the meeting of Board of Directors on 21st March, 2012, which is not in such a closer proximity to the JV agreement to raise any doubt about the intention of the PL behind the transfer of its assets to the BSPL. We note that neither of two forums below had given due and fair consideration to the facts and circumstances of the case and have arrived on the conclusion by picking a chunk of events which is supportive to their pre-determined conclusion. It is pertinent to point out here that the initial burden to prima facie prove that the intention of the PL at the date of decision of the BOD on 21st March, 2012 to transfer assets to BSPL was to avoid the incidence of Capital Gain Tax, and the idea of the JV partnership had already been conceived in the background by then. Nevertheless, we are unable to find any such evidence at all, to support such conclusion. All the evidence, that the DCIR and the CIR(A), have relied upon in arriving at their respective conclusions had. been based on the facts subsequent to the date of the actual date of execution of the asset transfer agreement. 

In view of the foregoing, we find that the revenue has failed to discharge its initial burden to prove that the purpose behind the transaction of transfer of asset by appellant PL to its wholly owned subsidiary BSPL was to avoidance or reduction of tax liability under the provisions of the Ordinance. 

22. For what has been discussed above and respectfully following the principles settled by the honourable Sindh High Court as well as the other precedents of the UK jurisdiction, we consider that transaction under consideration does not attract the mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance. We have no doubts in our minds that appellant's claim of tax-neutrality under section 97 of the Ordinance was bona fide, lawful and departmental action on this account was based on gross mis-appreciation of facts/ circumstances and a completely whimsical interpretation of the related statutory provisions. Accordingly, addition made in appellant's taxable income and consequential tax imposed on this account is deleted and orders of authorities below are vacated on this point. The grounds succeed. Since the main issue stands decided in appellant's favour, we do not consider it necessary to adjudicate the Grounds of appeal Nos. 4 to 6 taken by the appellant.”



From the records it transpires that the appellant sought exemption under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance and thereafter aligned itself to be eligible for the claim by formation of a Group and then aligned itself to seek Group Registration under the Rules with SECP and a Group return under section 59AA was filed for this year availing the exemption. Now the issue in appeal as raised by the Officer is that the taxpayer has sought which is not eligible as one of the entities in the Group is exempt from tax as well as it has not followed certain requirements. Hence the Officer is of the view that the claim of exemption and benefit under the law has been incorrectly availed and thus disregarded this in the Order in exercise of powers under section 109 of the Ordinance; these are reproduced below: 

“109. 	Recharacterisation of income and deductions. — (1) For the purposes of determining liability to tax under this Ordinance, the Commissioner may –

(a) 	recharacterise a transaction or an element of a transaction that was entered into as part of a tax avoidance scheme; 

(b) 	disregard a transaction that does not have substantial economic effect; or 

(c) 	recharacterise a transaction where the form of the transaction does not reflect the substance. 

(d)	from tax year 2018 and onwards, disregard an entity or a corporate structure that does not have an economic or commercial substance or was created as part of the tax avoidance scheme.

(2) In this section, “tax avoidance scheme” means any transaction where one of the main purposes of a person in entering into the transaction is the avoidance or reduction of any person’s liability to tax under this Ordinance. 

(3) Reduction in a person's liability to tax as referred to in sub-section (2) means a reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax or increase in a refund of tax and includes a reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax that would have been payable under this Ordinance, but are not payable due to a tax treaty for the avoidance of double taxation as referred to in section 107.”



56.	From the contents of the Order, I have reached the  conclusion that this matter has not been properly appreciated in the context of the framework of the law as provided including the Rules and thus the action taken is annulled with specific directions to frame a speaking order on the following pertinent aspects of invoking the provisions of the law and the role of SECP to revoke the Group Registration and designation of the appellant:

i.	Prime question is the identification of the underlying transaction which has been recharacterized in this case and whether the declaration as Group under section 59AA of the Ordinance by a regulatory authority under the powers exercised by it would qualify as a ‘transaction’?
ii.	In the absence of a transaction, whether there lies the jurisdiction for an action under section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance?
iii.	Whether or not there lies the jurisdiction for an action under section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance and to declare the claim of “exemption under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule” made by fulfilling the conditions of section 59AA of the Ordinance as a “tax avoidance scheme” as defined under section 109(2) of the Ordinance?
iv.	Whether there lies a jurisdiction under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance to disregard a Group Return filed under section 59AA of the Ordinance upon exercise of option after requisite approval by SECP?
v.	Whether or not the SECP has undertaken any action during the period in question for any non-compliance of regulation including compliance with Corporate Governance Regulations and applicable provision of the law to be invoked by the Officer if in case there is such a default?

Dear Walid,
Please refer to your request for our comments on taxability of fuel allowance, if UEP opts to give fuel to its employee via fuel card of oil marketing company’s [OMCs] like Shell or PSO. You have further informed us that the UEP will issue fuel cards to their employees and the cost of the fuel is reimbursed to the OMCs rather than to the employees. Any short consumption by the employee against his actual entitlement would be paid to the employee.

COMPANY MAINTAINED CAR WITH FUEL ALLOWANCE: 

In this context, where a benefit of car is provided by the UEP being the employer, it also includes the running and maintenance cost of such car. Accordingly, the cost of actual fuel used in such car is included in the taxable benefit computed under Rule 5 of Income Tax Rules, 2002. This rule provides the value of such benefit at 5% of the cost of vehicle to be included in the computation of taxable salary of the employee. Such notional amount, in our view, covers the repair and maintenance including periodic services, insurance, road tax beside actual fuel cost provided the Bank is either claiming refund of excess of allowance over actual expenditure or treating such excess as taxable benefit in the hands of employee. 

FUEL ALLOWANCE PROVIDED WITHOUT COMPANY MAINTAINED CAR: 

Nevertheless, where the benefit of a car is not provided by the UEP, then fuel cards can arguably be said to be a taxable perquisite to be added in the employee’s salary since any perquisite, whether convertible to money or not, received by an employee from any employment is covered within the definition of “salary” under section 12(2)(d) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. The said clause is also being reproduced below for quick reference:

“(d)	the amount of any expenditure incurred by an employee that is paid or reimbursed by the employer, other than expenditure incurred on behalf of the employer in the performance of the employee’s duties of employment”

The exception emphasized above is, as we understand, applicable only in certain cases where expenditure is incurred by the employee specifically towards the performance of office duties. For example, while being outstation or to travel from office to another location for the performance of office duties and vice versa. In such cases, to be able to claim exemption from salary tax, appropriate documentation supported with evidence wherever applicable should be present to be entitled to claim. Further, to avoid unwarranted inferences or queries in relation to tax avoidance HR policy should avoid any reference to ‘fuel allowance’ and clearly mention that the employee is entitled to fuel for official purpose for which the UEP has decided to use the methodology of fuel cards to employee. Having said that, fuel cards granted for general travel of the employee would remain a taxable perquisite. 

With respect to allowance against short consumption of the employee’s entitled limit, it would be clear that the allowance is not expended in the performance of the employee’s duties of employment, and therefore the same should be offered for tax as fuel allowance under section 12(2)(c) as advised earlier.

Hi Komal, 

Please refer to your email below through which you have requested us to provide views on the Sindh Sales Tax applicable on the renting of immovable properties after the recent decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan dated September 5, 2022. 

It is to be noted that the said judgment of SC has confirmed the earlier decision of the Sindh High Court (SHC) in case of Young's (Private) Limited. However, as you are already aware, to nullify the effect of the decision of SHC, the definition of “economic activity” provided in the section 4 of the Act was amended through the Sindh Sales Tax on Services (Amendment) Act, 2018 dated 11 April 2018 (with retrospective effect from 01 July 2015) which included renting of immovable property under the purview of economic activity. The earlier judgment of SHC held that renting of immovable property was neither a service nor taxable service or part of economic activity as defined. The Supreme Court in its judgment (while confirming the judgment of SHC) held that:
 
"2. Learned counsel for the appellant argued that renting of immovable property per se is a "taxable service" under section 3 of the Act and, therefore, liable to sales tax on services under section 8 of the Act. We have examined the impugned judgment in detail. The High Court, after an elaborate discussion, held that a cumulative reading of sections 2(728), 2(72C), 3, 4, 5 and 8 of the Act shows that "taxable service" is that which is provided by a registered person in the course of an economic activity from his registered office or place of business in Sindh. What the appellants want to tax is not taxable service liable to taxation under the Act. The mere renting out of property by a landlord to a tenant is not taxable as it is not a taxable service.

3. The grounds raised by the appellants have been convincingly answered in the impugned judgment. We are in complete agreement with the learned Judges of the High Court and see no reason to take a view different from the one taken by the High Court in its well-reasoned judgment or the necessity to further elaborate on any aspect of the matter. The listed appeals are, therefore, dismissed."

The SC has, as emphasized above, in the first part confirmed the view that mere renting of immovable property is not a taxable service. This first part of judgement may be argued as dependent upon un-amended definition of economic activity (which effectively form part of definition of taxable service). Therefore, to that extent it may be argued that the said part of the judgment may not be squarely applicable in the post-amended era.

However, in the second part, as emphasized above, SC has shown complete agreement with the judgement of SHC, which had also held that renting of immovable property is not a “service”. This inference can be drawn and applicable even now as this interpretation is based on general connotation of the term “services”, still unaffected by any legislative amendment.

Therefore, based on above, we are of the view that SCs decision would be applicable post amendment Act of 2018 and as a result, SST can be argued as not applicable on renting of immovable property.

It may however be noted that post amendment Act of 2018, when SRB approached taxpayers (that SST is applicable on renting of immovable property as it has now cured the lacuna in law, in their view, as identified by SHC), the tenants as well as landlords challenged the same in SHC and obtained interim stay orders. Since the matter is still pending before SHC and the Bank is a withholding agent, it would be appropriate for the Bank in cases where there is no stay order of High Court, to either withhold sales tax or obtain undertaking from the landlord that they will be responsible for the liability of SST if SRB approach them for non-withholding of SST.

Since the matter also involves interpretation of judgment of the Supreme Court, the Bank may also seek the opinion of its legal counsel on the matter.

“29. The taxpayer’s reply on the issue of ‘group taxation/ intercorporate dividend exemption’ has been perused and placed on record. i. The sub rule (4) of the Rule 231D of the Income Tax Rules 2002 requires that ‘the holding company as well as each subsidiary company shall furnish a certificate issued by the SECP verifying that the company has been complying with the Code of Corporate Governance as notified from time to time by the SECP.

iii. 	Both above legal provisions mandatorily require the companies opting for group taxation to comply with such corporate governance requirements and group designation rules or regulations as may be specified by the SECP and furnish such certificates issued by the SECP. The taxpayer at serial number (vi) of the table given at para 12 of its reply dated January 25, 2021 has admitted that no such certificates have been issued to it or its subsidiary company. iv. 	The taxpayer’s excuse that due to status of the taxpayer and its subsidiary company being ‘Public Unlisted Companies’ the SECP law/ rules are not applicable in its case and it does not disqualify the taxpayer and its subsidiary from group taxation is not maintainable because the Income Tax Law and the rules there under clearly precondition such requirement. The law says the companies opting for group taxation SHALL COMPLY WITH the applicable ‘Codes of Corporate Governance’ as notified time to time by the SECP and SHALL avail such compliance certificate from the SECP. Non availability of compliance certificate with the Codes of Corporate Governance by the SECP means the taxpayer does not qualify for group taxation.

v. Without prejudice to above, the option for ‘Group Taxation’ u/s 59AA of the Ordinance is available for the Holding Companies and their 100% owned subsidiaries whose incomes are taxable. For ready reference the substantive provisions of section 59AA of the Ordinance are reproduced for ready reference as under:

“Section 59AA. Group taxation. — (1) Holding companies and subsidiary companies of 100% owned group may opt to be taxed as one fiscal unit. In such cases, besides consolidated group accounts as required under the Companies Ordinance, 1984 (XLVII of 1984), computation of income and tax payable shall be made for tax purposes”.

vi. Plain reading of the above reproduced provisions of the law vividly transpires that:

a. Option for group taxation is for ‘to be taxed as one fiscal unit’.

b. Further the law requires that in such cases (consolidated) computation of income and tax payable
shall be made for tax purposes.

When the law provides that Holding and 100% owned subsidiary companies may opt for TO BE TAXED AS SIGNGLE FISCAL UNIT and COMPUTATION OF INCOME AND TAX PAYABLE SHALL BE MADE FOR TAX PURPOSES then it is very clear that the option for group taxation is allowable to those companies whose incomes are taxable under the Ordinance. The law clearly excludes those companies from opting group taxation whose incomes are exempt from tax. The taxpayer’s claim that there is no explicit restricting provisions actually shows its poor understanding of the law. Therefore, the taxpayer’s option for ‘group taxation’ u/s 59AA of the Ordinance is void ab initio.

Accordingly, the return filed under group taxation is disallowed/ disregarded for the law, facts of the case and reasons thereof discussed above and in terms of section 109(1) (a) & (b) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 (as the taxpayer has tried to avoid tax due through the arrangements neither supported by the law or confirmed by SECP). Hence, the taxpayer is not entitled to claim any exemption on interoperate dividend. The assessment of the subsidiary is to be done on the basis of its return of income.

30. The case laws relied upon by the taxpayer are not related to the facts of taxpayer’s case and distinguishable both on the planes of facts of the cases and the applicable provisions of the law.”

(ii)	High Court of Sindh reported as 2018 PTD 114 in the case of IGI Insurance Company Limited

(iii)	Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue in the case of M/s Uni Brands Pvt. Ltd. in ITA 64/KB/2021 and MA(AG) No. 1540/KB/2021 dated July 14, 2022

(iv)	Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue in the case of M/s Aitkenstuart Pakistan (Private) Limited in ITA No. 846/KB.2022

(ii)	Listed Companies (Code of Corporate Governance) Regulations, 2019



FINDINGS

50.	I have perused the detailed written submissions of the AR both on legal and factual plaints and considered the same in conjunction with the action of the ACIR of rejecting the “irrevocable” Group Taxation Option to dislodge the claim of exemption under clause 103 A of Part I of the Second Schedule. Before me, the question is whether the claim of an exemption on intercorporate dividend income under clause 103A of Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance after fulfilling the condition of filing a Group Return on formation of a Group as approved by the SECP under section 59AA of the Ordinance, could be rejected after exercise of the provisions of section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance. 

51.	The provision of law allowing exemption for the period is as under:

“(103A) Any income derived from inter-corporate dividend within the group companies entitled to group taxation under section 59AA subject to the condition that return of the group has been filed for the tax year.”


52.	I have carefully considered these provisions of clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance which grant exemption on filing Group return under section 59AA of the Ordinance read with Rule 231D and the SECP Group Companies Registration Regulations, 2008 issued in this regard. These provisions are self-contained code of law entitling the persons eligible for the concession. It appears that these permit, empower or allow a process for rejection of the Option for taxation as a unit under section 59AA(2) of the Ordinance once this Group was so designated and registered by the SECP, section 59AA(5) of the Ordinance provides as under:  

“(5) The option of group taxation shall be available to those group companies which comply with such corporate governance requirements and group designation rules or regulations as may be specified by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan from time to time and are designated as companies entitled to avail group taxation.”

53.	A reading of all these provisions seems to lead to the conclusion that the powers to designate and register a Group or to disband it lies with the SECP as the requirements to form and operate a Group are enlisted in the Rules issued by the SECP; non-compliance of which will lead to the deregistration of the Group after appropriate proceedings by the SECP. Moreover, under Rule 231D(8) of Income Tax Rules, 2002 it has been identified as under: 

“(8) In case, there is divestment of a subsidiary company and the provisions of group taxation become inapplicable, no effect shall be taken for group taxation during the year of disposal.”


54.	Next ,I have also carefully considered the provisions for invoking and application of section 109 (1)(a) and (b) which lay down that transactions need to be undertaken to avoid the tax due as well as the interpretation of the Sindh High Court in the case reported as 2018 PTD 114 as well as in ITA No. 723/KB/2018 reported (2022) 125 Tax 132 (Trib.) where this the matter of “tax avoidance and section 109 is discussed in detail as quoted below:

“18.	It is manifestly clear that no hard and fast rules or principles could be laid down where a provision of law is required to be construed purposively. Each and every case needs to be considered on its own facts and circumstance. The qualification and disqualification would always remain dependent on facts and circumstances of each case. We now proceed with applying the above authoritatively, unambiguously and unequivocally settled principles on the facts of the present case. In this regard, it would be in the fitness of things if the contentions of the authorities below as recorded in their respective orders, and reproduced above, are also kept in consideration. In the present case, it is patently clear that the transfer· of assets was necessitated owing to certain very pertinent business reasons. All documents on record, including, intimations to regulatory authorities and shareholders loudly and clearly depicted the underlying main purpose and objective of the complete transactions i.e., proceeding with inclusion of a joint venture partner well before the actual transaction affecting transfer of assets. As is evident from the amendment order and other assessment records, appellant has made strategic investments in various projects and in certain cases also engaged foreign partners in various business ventures. The primary purpose of subject transfer was also predominantly to bring foreign investment & foreign expertise in one of the lines of appellant's business i.e., Paper & Board and Corrugated business and for this reason, existing business was restructured by way of hive down of relevant assets into BSPL with subsequent induction of a Joint Venture partner (i.e., Stora Enso) therein. Thus, we fully concur with the learned AR's View that the overarching purpose of the transaction was nothing but business/economic consideration ultimately aimed at enrichment of business and shareholder value and was not meant wholly and exclusively for avoidance of any tax, as has been asserted by department. while the department has tried to make out a case that the series of events i.e., from the date of announcement of transfer of assets to BSPL till issuance of equity to Stora enso, constituted ‘pre-ordinated transactions’ aimed at avoidance of tax in terms of the judgements of UK jurisdiction, if has relied to appreciate the position that it is a considered view of Courts that only such transaction can attract GAAR application, whose main objective is avoidance of tax, which we have no doubts in our minds, is not the case here. The claim of tax neutrality under section 97 of the Ordinance it is apt to be noted, was only, at best, 'incidental' to achievement of appellant's main business purpose. Accordingly, in terms of ratio decidendi of the order of the Sindh High Court this transaction, holistically speaking, is not hit by the mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance.

19.	The assertion of revenue that in a series of transactions where any one individual transaction results into non imposition of tax otherwise leviable under the statute, mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance is fully applicable is, in our view, not only seriously flawed but also offends the principles settled by their lordships in order of Sindh High Court referred supra. If this was considered to be permissible, or for that matter, intent of legislature then practically all provisions extending any benefit, incentive, advantage etc. would become meaningless and redundant. Every such claim could then be disputed on notions and hypothesis. In terms of scheme envisaged in the statute benefits/concessions stipulated in sections 95, 96, 97, 97A or for that matter under sections 59AA or 59B of the Ordinance, cannot be denied without undertaking complete analysis through a purposive approach, as eloquently deliberated in the judgement cited supra. To elaborate, every action by taxpayers to undertake business re-organizations or to make them eligible for any tax mitigation / concessions etc, could not be, per se, dragged in the provisions of section 109 of the Ordinance, unit, and unless the analysis of facts/circumstances & underlying objectives indicate that principal purpose thereof is tax avoidance. If this process could be allowed to be bypassed or short circuited, the ultimate result would be that the entire super structure of law setting out benefits and advantages etc. could crumble. This, we consider, is obviously neither the  legislative intent nor a purposive interpretation of the statutory provisions. It is in this background that it is a considered view of Court that ‘tax mitigation’ and ‘tax avoidance’ need to be necessarily differentiated whilst applying the GAAR provisions and it is only in case of the latter that these come into play and that too in circumstances where the primary purpose of executing the transaction, and not the incidental purpose is 'tax avoidance'. The entire edifice built by revenue while invoking provisions of section 109 of the Ordinance in the present case is self-contradictory when at one hand the department treats transfer under section 97 of the Ordinance as hit by the mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance and in the same breath concedes that the transaction would have been tax neutral had the objective of transaction been achieved under section 97 A of the Ordinance. It is not understandable as to how, according to revenue, invocation of section 97 A of the Ordinance would have cleared the transaction from the scope of section 109 of the Ordinance when the ultimate objective of transfer of assets had stood at par as is under current circumstances.”


55.	The concluding paragraphs from the Order are as under:

“…….. However, in our opinion, under the facts of the case, this conclusion is unsafe, when there is evidence available of the fact that though the agreement to transfer assets of 15th September, 2012 was made merely two months prior to the Joint venture agreement of 15th November, 2012, however, the original decision to transfer the assets was made by the PL in the meeting of Board of Directors on 21st March, 2012, which is not in such a closer proximity to the JV agreement to raise any doubt about the intention of the PL behind the transfer of its assets to the BSPL. We note that neither of two forums below had given due and fair consideration to the facts and circumstances of the case and have arrived on the conclusion by picking a chunk of events which is supportive to their pre-determined conclusion. It is pertinent to point out here that the initial burden to prima facie prove that the intention of the PL at the date of decision of the BOD on 21st March, 2012 to transfer assets to BSPL was to avoid the incidence of Capital Gain Tax, and the idea of the JV partnership had already been conceived in the background by then. Nevertheless, we are unable to find any such evidence at all, to support such conclusion. All the evidence, that the DCIR and the CIR(A), have relied upon in arriving at their respective conclusions had. been based on the facts subsequent to the date of the actual date of execution of the asset transfer agreement. 

In view of the foregoing, we find that the revenue has failed to discharge its initial burden to prove that the purpose behind the transaction of transfer of asset by appellant PL to its wholly owned subsidiary BSPL was to avoidance or reduction of tax liability under the provisions of the Ordinance. 

22. For what has been discussed above and respectfully following the principles settled by the honourable Sindh High Court as well as the other precedents of the UK jurisdiction, we consider that transaction under consideration does not attract the mischief of section 109 of the Ordinance. We have no doubts in our minds that appellant's claim of tax-neutrality under section 97 of the Ordinance was bona fide, lawful and departmental action on this account was based on gross mis-appreciation of facts/ circumstances and a completely whimsical interpretation of the related statutory provisions. Accordingly, addition made in appellant's taxable income and consequential tax imposed on this account is deleted and orders of authorities below are vacated on this point. The grounds succeed. Since the main issue stands decided in appellant's favour, we do not consider it necessary to adjudicate the Grounds of appeal Nos. 4 to 6 taken by the appellant.”



From the records it transpires that the appellant sought exemption under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance and thereafter aligned itself to be eligible for the claim by formation of a Group and then aligned itself to seek Group Registration under the Rules with SECP and a Group return under section 59AA was filed for this year availing the exemption. Now the issue in appeal as raised by the Officer is that the taxpayer has sought which is not eligible as one of the entities in the Group is exempt from tax as well as it has not followed certain requirements. Hence the Officer is of the view that the claim of exemption and benefit under the law has been incorrectly availed and thus disregarded this in the Order in exercise of powers under section 109 of the Ordinance; these are reproduced below: 

“109. 	Recharacterisation of income and deductions. — (1) For the purposes of determining liability to tax under this Ordinance, the Commissioner may –

(a) 	recharacterise a transaction or an element of a transaction that was entered into as part of a tax avoidance scheme; 

(b) 	disregard a transaction that does not have substantial economic effect; or 

(c) 	recharacterise a transaction where the form of the transaction does not reflect the substance. 

(d)	from tax year 2018 and onwards, disregard an entity or a corporate structure that does not have an economic or commercial substance or was created as part of the tax avoidance scheme.

(2) In this section, “tax avoidance scheme” means any transaction where one of the main purposes of a person in entering into the transaction is the avoidance or reduction of any person’s liability to tax under this Ordinance. 

(3) Reduction in a person's liability to tax as referred to in sub-section (2) means a reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax or increase in a refund of tax and includes a reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax that would have been payable under this Ordinance, but are not payable due to a tax treaty for the avoidance of double taxation as referred to in section 107.”



56.	From the contents of the Order, I have reached the  conclusion that this matter has not been properly appreciated in the context of the framework of the law as provided including the Rules and thus the action taken is annulled with specific directions to frame a speaking order on the following pertinent aspects of invoking the provisions of the law and the role of SECP to revoke the Group Registration and designation of the appellant:

i.	Prime question is the identification of the underlying transaction which has been recharacterized in this case and whether the declaration as Group under section 59AA of the Ordinance by a regulatory authority under the powers exercised by it would qualify as a ‘transaction’?
ii.	In the absence of a transaction, whether there lies the jurisdiction for an action under section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance?
iii.	Whether or not there lies the jurisdiction for an action under section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance and to declare the claim of “exemption under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule” made by fulfilling the conditions of section 59AA of the Ordinance as a “tax avoidance scheme” as defined under section 109(2) of the Ordinance?
iv.	Whether there lies a jurisdiction under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance to disregard a Group Return filed under section 59AA of the Ordinance upon exercise of option after requisite approval by SECP?
v.	Whether or not the SECP has undertaken any action during the period in question for any non-compliance of regulation including compliance with Corporate Governance Regulations and applicable provision of the law to be invoked by the Officer if in case there is such a default?

**Comments on Ground of Appeal No. 7 and Findings of the Commissioner (Appeals):**

**Ground of Appeal No. 7 – Group Taxation and Section 109 of the Ordinance:**

The appellant contests the rejection of the Group Return filed under section 59AA of the Ordinance, which included its wholly owned subsidiary. This rejection resulted in the taxation of the Intercorporate Dividend claimed as exempt under clause 103A of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance.

The ACIR's rejection was based on the appellant's failure to comply with corporate governance requirements specified by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) and the ineligibility to form a group with an entity whose profits are tax-exempt. The appellant argues that the ACIR wrongly assumed the power to reject the "irrevocable" Group option and taxed the dividend income claimed exempt.

**Comments on Commissioner's Findings:**

The Commissioner's findings indicate a legal and procedural analysis of the rejection of the Group Return and the subsequent taxation of the claimed exemption. The Commissioner relies on specific provisions of the Ordinance and Rules, emphasizing the mandatory nature of compliance with SECP regulations for group taxation eligibility.

The Commissioner invokes section 109(1)(a) and (b) of the Ordinance, suggesting that the taxpayer attempted to avoid tax through arrangements not supported by law or confirmed by the SECP. The Commissioner also refers to the substantive provisions of section 59AA, emphasizing that group taxation is available to companies with taxable incomes, excluding those with exempt incomes.

The appellant argues that the ACIR lacks the authority to reject the Group Option once exercised, highlighting that no objections were raised by the department when the option was exercised. Additionally, the appellant contends that SECP has the sole authority to disintegrate groups formed under its regulations.

The appellant further disputes the application of section 109(1)(a) and (b), asserting that the formation of the group was a necessary business exigency rather than a tax avoidance scheme. The appellant also relies on legal precedents to differentiate between tax mitigation and tax avoidance.

The Commissioner's findings emphasize the need for SECP compliance, linking it to the eligibility for group taxation and subsequent tax exemption. The Commissioner contends that SECP, not the tax authorities, has the jurisdiction to cancel group registrations based on non-compliance.

The appellant raises valid points challenging the ACIR's authority to reject the Group Option and disputes the characterization of their actions as a tax avoidance scheme. The appellant relies on legal precedents to argue that the primary purpose of the transaction was business/economic considerations rather than tax avoidance.

The Commissioner is directed to reevaluate the case, considering the specific questions raised by the appellant regarding the identification of underlying transactions, the jurisdiction for action under section 109, and the role of SECP in revoking group registration.

Dear [Commissioner's Name],

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing on behalf of [Appellant's Name], and I would like to bring to your attention certain crucial aspects related to the disallowance of the windfall levy amounting to Rs 3,170,249,484, under section 34(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance.

During the hearing, the Appellant's Representative (AR) argued that the Assessing Officer (ACIR) erred in disallowing the windfall levy on the basis that the expense is merely a provision. The AR contended that, as the books of accounts of the Appellant are maintained under the mercantile/accrual system of accounting, the deduction under the head of Windfall Levy is valid.

The relevant sections of the Income Tax Ordinance, specifically sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 32, emphasize that a company shall account for income on an accrual basis. This is in line with Rule 32 of the Rules, requiring the maintenance of books of accounts in accordance with the International Accounting Standards (IAS).

The Appellant draws your attention to the ITAT Islamabad decision in the case of M/s. Fauji Fertilizer Company Limited (Ref ITA No. 317(IB)/85-86), where it was established that an expenditure is allowable on an accrual basis, even if the actual payment is made at a later date.

Furthermore, judicial precedents such as the Sindh High Court's decision (97 TAX 301) and the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal's ruling (1981) 44 TAX 62, support the claim that if a taxpayer follows the mercantile basis of accounting, they are entitled to a deduction for accrued liabilities, such as bonus, even if not paid during the year.

A noteworthy decision is the one from the High Court of Sindh, Karachi, where the court upheld the ITAT decision in favor of Union Texas Pakistan Inc, stating that there is no condition regarding the ultimate utilization or distribution of the amount allocated to the Fund.

In light of these legal precedents and the fact that the Appellant maintains accounts on a mercantile system, it is evident that the provision for the windfall levy, being a definite and ascertained amount, is valid and should be allowed as an accrued liability.

Moreover, the Appellant's reliance on recent decisions such as M/s MOL Pakistan Oil & Gas Co. B.V versus CIR, LTU, Islamabad, and M/s National Foods Ltd, wherein the ITAT allowed expenses on the basis of incurrence, adds strength to their case.

Considering the above, it is respectfully requested to reconsider the disallowance of the windfall levy and acknowledge the validity of the provision made under the accrual system.

I am writing in response to your email dated January 4, 2024, wherein you sought our opinion on the eligibility of a dean—primarily engaged in teaching duties while also overseeing certain academic functions at the University—for the concessional provision outlined in Clause 2 of Part III of the Second Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Ordinance).

In consideration of your query, it is pertinent to refer to Circular No. 06 of 2013 issued by the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) on July 19, 2013. The circular provides clarification on the definition of a full-time teacher, specifying that it encompasses individuals employed exclusively for teaching and excludes those involved in any administrative or managerial roles. Such roles may include principals, headmasters, directors, vice-chancellors, chairpersons, controllers, and similar positions. Likewise, the definition extends to full-time researchers, who are individuals solely employed for research activities within institutions dedicated to research.

Given the guidance provided by the FBR and considering the specific circumstances outlined in your inquiry, it becomes evident that individuals combining administrative responsibilities with their primary role as teachers may not qualify for the benefits stipulated in Clause 2 of Part III of the Second Schedule to the Ordinance.

Subject: Taxability of Fuel Allowance via Fuel Cards

Dear Walid,

I trust this message finds you well. In response to your inquiry regarding the taxability of fuel allowance, particularly when UEP opts to provide fuel to its employees through fuel cards issued by oil marketing companies such as Shell or PSO, we have conducted a thorough review.

1. **Company Maintained Car with Fuel Allowance:**
   In situations where UEP provides the benefit of a company-maintained car, including covering the running and maintenance costs, the actual fuel cost used in the car is considered a taxable benefit. Rule 5 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002, specifies that 5% of the vehicle's cost should be included in the computation of the employee's taxable salary. This notional amount is deemed to cover repair and maintenance, insurance, road tax, and actual fuel costs. It is crucial that any excess allowance over actual expenditure is either claimed for refund or treated as a taxable benefit in the hands of the employee.

2. **Fuel Allowance Provided Without Company Maintained Car:**
   In cases where UEP does not provide the benefit of a company-maintained car, fuel cards can be deemed a taxable perquisite and added to the employee's salary. Section 12(2)(d) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, defines "salary" to include any expenditure incurred by an employee paid or reimbursed by the employer. The exception to this rule applies when the expenditure is incurred specifically for the performance of office duties, and appropriate documentation with evidence must be maintained to claim exemption. It is advisable for HR policies to avoid explicitly referencing 'fuel allowance' and clarify that the employee is entitled to fuel for official purposes, using the fuel card methodology. However, fuel cards granted for general employee travel remain a taxable perquisite.

Regarding the allowance for short consumption against the employee's entitled limit, it is important to note that such allowance is not expended in the performance of the employee's duties of employment. Therefore, it should be treated as fuel allowance under section 12(2)(c) and offered for tax, as advised earlier.

I hope this clarifies the tax implications of fuel allowance via fuel cards. Should you have any further questions or require additional information, please feel free to reach out.
